h2: Magnetic particle testing myths, from ASTM E709 to demagnetization
html:
Magnetic particle testing myths, from ASTM E709 to demagnetization

MT looks simple, which is why it collects myths. Most come from mixing up the documents, trusting a field nobody verified, or reading every line of particles as a crack. The cross-method list is in conventional NDT myths.

Myth: ASTM E709, or "ASME E709", is the MT standard you must follow

E709 is an ASTM guide: a reference that describes dry and wet techniques and helps people write specifications and procedures. ASTM E1444/E1444M is the practice that sets minimum requirements, and its current edition describes E709 as a companion tutorial. There is no separate "ASME E709". ASME reproduces the guide as SE-709 in Section V, but the mandatory ASME rules for MT sit in Section V Article 7, and acceptance comes from the construction code. Cite Article 7 or E1444 for requirements, E709 for guidance, and the acceptance code by name.

Myth: Paint can always stay on

ASTM E709 notes that thin nonconductive coatings, around 1 to 2 mils (0.02 to 0.05 mm), do not normally stop indications forming. Thicker coatings hold the particles away from the leakage field, and conductive coatings can mask flaws. Where a coating stays on, the procedure should require a demonstration that indications are detected through the maximum coating thickness present, and the coating must come off wherever current passes into the part, as with prods. Measure the coating with a gauge and record it on the report.

Myth: Every line of particles is a crack

Particles gather wherever flux leaks, and not all leakage comes from flaws. Non-relevant indications form at abrupt section changes, keyways and threads, along the bond line between carbon steel and an austenitic weld or the edge of a heat-affected zone, where permeability changes, and as "magnetic writing" where a magnetized part touched other steel. An excessive field makes particles cling along surface texture too. A Level II separates relevant from non-relevant indications by checking geometry and material, wiping and retesting, or confirming with penetrant testing. Record why each call was judged non-relevant.

Myth: More current and more particles give better results

Too much field saturates the part and builds a heavy background that buries fine indications, and too many particles in a wet fluorescent (WFMT) or visible bath do the same. Quality Magazine's column on MT misunderstandings lists both as common mistakes. Set the field for the part, its geometry and the expected flaw, verify it, and check bath concentration at the interval the procedure sets. If the background is heavy, the answer is a cleaner bath or a lower setting, not a longer look.

Myth: A pie gauge measures field strength

A pie-shaped field indicator shows that a field exists at the surface and roughly which way it runs; it does not measure strength. Iowa State's NDE-Ed resource notes that there is no easy way to measure field intensity at a point inside a part. Artificial-flaw shims with notches of known depth are a better check that the field is adequate in a given direction, and a Hall-effect gaussmeter reads the tangential field at the surface where a specification asks for a number. Use the indicator your procedure names, on the part, at the area being examined, not on a test plate across the shop.

Myth: Demagnetization is always required, or never needed

Neither. Demagnetize when residual magnetism would cause trouble later: arc blow during welding, chips clinging during machining, interference with instruments, particles drawn into bearings, or a following MT shot in another direction. The procedure states when demagnetization is required and the residual-field limit, checked with a field meter. Low-carbon steels often hold little residual field, but measure rather than assume. Teach technicians to make these calls with magnetic particle testing training, let them practise on the MT simulator, and have procedures written and approved through NDT procedure development. For weld work, see magnetic particle weld inspection.
